papers.title: EXPRESS: Impatient for Impact: Intertemporal Preferences for Earlier Donation Impact Timing
papers.abstract: Impatience when choosing for oneself has been widely documented, but are people also impatient when making prosocial decisions about benefits to unknown others? The authors study whether and why people care about a donation’s “impact timing,” the time when the benefits of the donation would reach the beneficiaries. In seven pre-registered experiments (N = 2,462) and an analysis of GoFundMe secondary data, they show that people consistently prefer to donate to a charitable program with an earlier impact timing, across different causes, donation amounts, timeframes, charity sizes and tradeoffs between impact timing and other considerations (impact magnitude, number of prior donors, remaining cost to complete, quality rating, and overhead). They find that decreased perceived benefits of delayed donation impact provides an incomplete explanation of the impact timing preference. Beyond less discounting of less delayed benefits, people also infer greater donation efficacy-based trust from earlier impact timing, increasing donation preferences. Together, the strong preference for earlier impact timing is an important and largely overlooked aspect of prosocial decision-making, with implications for building trust in prosocial organizations.

papers.title: EXPRESS: When Marketers Get the Top Job: How Marketing CEOs Influence Firms’ Product-Market Strategy
papers.authors: Shekhar Misra, Ben Lee, Christophe Haon
papers.abstract: Research on upper echelons in marketing has primarily focused on the CMO, yet the CEO ultimately bears responsibility for key strategic decisions, including those related to marketing. This study examines how CEOs with marketing experience (i.e., “marketing CEOs”) influence firm stock market performance by shaping product portfolio decisions. Drawing on upper echelon theory and in-depth interviews with business practitioners, we argue that marketing CEOs are more effective at selecting customer segments and implementing competitive strategies, leading to more differentiated portfolios and, consequently, higher shareholder returns. Our analysis of the main research question combines a qualitative study, a natural experiment involving CEO turnovers, large-scale panel data analysis, and an experiment with executives. Our results show that marketing CEOs positively impact shareholder returns through portfolio differentiation. Furthermore, the positive effect of marketing CEOs on portfolio differentiation is strengthened by their larger professional networks and a strong customer orientation within the firm but is diminished by CEO overconfidence and high firm financial leverage. Our findings highlight the distinctive value of CEOs with marketing experience and provide insight into the conditions that enhance or constrain their ability to generate firm value.

papers.title: Swap and Save: How a Button Shapes Lasting Online Grocery Shopping Behavior
papers.authors: Rubén Gonzálvez, Xiaolin Li, Sarit Weisburd, Xinrong Zhu
papers.abstract: Using data from the mineral water category on a price comparison platform that delivers real-time prompts of cheaper alternatives through “swap and save” buttons, this study examines whether and how these prompts influence persistent product choices in online grocery shopping.

papers.title: EXPRESS: Are Exposure Bucks Worth It? Evidence from Instagram
papers.abstract: We estimate the benefit to creators of making collaborative posts with brands on Instagram, a feature that allows brands and creators to co-author shared posts. We link all collaborative posts from 260 leading fashion and beauty brands to a daily panel of follower counts for small-to-mid-tier collaborating creators, match treated and control posts on visual content, and exploit rigidity in brands' posting schedules to identify causal treatment effects in a difference-in-differences design. Collaborative posts increase a creator's cumulative follower count by 0.52% on average—roughly equivalent to one week of organic growth—with no effect on follower engagement or creators' propensity to partner with other brands. Heterogeneity analyses suggest that the primary benefit stems from audience exposure rather than quality signaling. While brands with larger follower bases yield larger gains all else being equal, they also have less engaged audiences and publish collaborative content that deviates further from creators' typical styles; as a result, treatment effects remain roughly constant across brands ranging from 0.7 to 8.6 million followers. Overall, collaborative posts provide relatively small exposure benefits to creators on average, but partnerships with brands that have highly engaged audiences and grant creative freedom deliver substantially greater value.

papers.title: EXPRESS: So Near Yet So Far: The Unexpected Role of Near Misses for Salesperson Turnover
papers.authors: Arpit Agrawal, Michael Ahearne, Yashar Atefi, Johannes Habel, Mohsen Pourmasoudi, Praveen Punia
papers.abstract: Quota attainment is critical for salespeople because it determines their income, recognition, and career progression. Accordingly, salespeople who frequently fail to meet quota may become more inclined to turn over and try their luck elsewhere. However, not all quota failures carry the same weight. Drawing on the expected utility model of turnover, we argue that salespeople who repeatedly miss quota by a narrow margin are especially likely to turn over. This is because such near misses erode a salesperson’s confidence that they will yield valued outcomes in their current job while increasing the perceived attainability of those outcomes elsewhere. We validate these predictions using a seven-year cross-industry panel of 13,277 salespeople across 44 companies, three experiments, and multiple auxiliary studies. The effect is stronger when hitting quota is more important due to high variable pay and group performance homogeneity. Furthermore, we establish expected utility of switching as the mechanism underlying these effects. Our research introduces near misses as a novel antecedent of turnover and as a new trigger that can reshape expected utilities. Furthermore, our research allows managers to implement targeted interventions to retain valuable talents, such as preventing near misses or reframing salespeople’s expected utility once near misses occur.

papers.title: EXPRESS: The Enjoy-Able Effect: Consumer Enjoyment Inflates Self-Evaluations of Ability
papers.authors: JACOB D. TEENY, DANIEL M. ZANE, ANNA PALEY, ROBERT W. SMITH
papers.abstract:
This research establishes the
                    enjoy-able effect
                    . Enjoyment (whether experienced, anticipated, or relative) increases consumers’ self-evaluated ability, leading them to act more like self-perceived experts (e.g., choose more expert-targeted products) and exhibit better-than-average biases for more enjoyable activities. Two waves of archival data (Ns = 559,370 and 491,791), normed associations across 100 consumer activities (N = 397), and six experiments (Ns = 251–593) document these outcomes of consumer enjoyment, establish that they operate independently of actual ability, and provide evidence that consumers’ inferences about their ability are driven by their overgeneralization of a lay theory about the relationship between enjoyment and expertise. The enjoy-able effect therefore depends on the diagnosticity of enjoyment as an input to subjective expertise, relative to other accessible inputs. Accordingly, this work highlights when and for whom other accessible inputs (e.g., an alternate lay theory associating effort and expertise) reduce reliance on the “enjoyment = expertise” lay theory. Overall, this research documents a previously unrecognized influence of enjoyment on consumer behavior, offers new insights on classic theories (e.g., flow and self-determination theory), and identifies a new and robust antecedent to subjective expertise. Managerial implications for product development and promotion, consumer targeting, and gamification are discussed.

papers.title: Overall Evaluation Criteria for A/B Tests: A Meta-Analytic Approach
papers.authors: Easton Huch, Stephanie A. Nail, Terran Melconian, Xan Vongsathorn, Fred Feinberg
papers.abstract: This paper discusses meta-analytic methods for estimating the value of marketing interventions given a database of historical A/B tests with multiple outcome variables.
